---
title: "Stage 6 — execute, and get a number"
---

Running the specification against real data, in the browser.

## What this is

The analysis runs under WebR — R compiled to WebAssembly — so nothing needs installing. The
data goes in as ADaM in transport format.

**This stage assumes you have analysis datasets.** That is worth saying, because the previous
five do not. Stages 0 to 5 need a protocol and a set of definitions; this one needs subject-level
data, in the browser, in a format the engine reads.

If you have none, the chain is not wasted — the output of stage 5 is a specification complete
enough for a programmer to implement, and that is arguably the deliverable. **Executing it
proves the specification is complete; it is not what the specification is for.** A reader with a
protocol and no data can follow every stage up to here and have something real at the end of it.

If you have data but not in this shape, the work is conversion rather than authoring: collected
data standardised to SDTM, derived to ADaM, and converted to transport format. That path is not
covered here.

## What you do

**The work:** run the declared specification against real subject-level data, and keep the
record of *how* it was run — every filter and join applied — because that record, not the
number, is what the next stage needs.

1. Make the analysis data available to the engine.
2. Execute the chain.
3. Keep the execution log, not just the result.

*In the application used here:* step 8, where the datasets are loaded into the browser and the
engine starts by downloading the R runtime on first use, so it takes a moment.

**The second number exists because this project wrote the implementation.** At the pinned
commit the library ships the MMRM template and the method definition, and no implementation in
R or SAS: Execute answers *No R implementation available for M.MMRM*. One was written here, in
the registry's own shape, and the walkthrough injects it into the running page, which is the
only reason a reader's copy can produce the figure above. Writing it took three iterations,
each a fact about the seam between the engine's data layer and a real mixed model: two rows at
baseline per subject, which a linear model had silently taken the first of and a mixed model
refuses; a derived column name the model's formula parser cannot use; and type-3 tests, which
needed a different route than the linear model's. Expect the same seam under any method the
library defines and does not implement.

### Step into the factory

Every figure above is read live from the run it came from. The runs and the chains are in
`endpoints/01-simple-lab-cfb/` and `endpoints/04-vitals-cfb-mmrm/`; the implementation is
`r_impl_mmrm.json` beside the vitals chain. The lessons below are item L7 in the lab endpoint's
`log.md`, with its decision table, and items V4 and V5 in the vitals endpoint's.

## What to look out for

**Execution takes decisions of its own, and none of them is statistical.** The lab endpoint
took eleven here, after a chain that stages 3 to 5 had passed as complete: which dataset, which
treatment variable, which population flag, which form of the parameter and visit dimensions and
which value of each, which covariate column. Every one is about a column or a label. Four exist
only because the study definition and the chain name things differently from the data. The
vitals endpoint took sixteen across its stages, ten of them already made once. Keep the record
of them with the result, because the next stage is about the choices, not the number.

**A clean run with the default covariate can be the wrong model.** The engine's default for
the covariate was the analysis value — which, for a change-from-baseline chain, is the
response's own minuend. The third run here executed without complaint on exactly that model.
The covariate has to be set to the baseline value by hand, and nothing flags the run that did
not.

*True of the application described here, at the pinned commit.*

**One choice is never offered.** Which record is the baseline — the first in the window or the
one a flag marks — is not a decision the engine puts to you; it takes the first. The divergence
the next chapter takes apart could not have been prevented here by a careful reader, because
there was nothing to be careful about. That is why it is a lesson about declaration rather than
about care.

**Read the contrast label, never assume the direction.** The stored contrast here is placebo
minus treatment, which is the opposite of how a report would usually phrase it. Quote the
label alongside the estimate and the sign cannot be got wrong — which is exactly why this
guide prints both from the data rather than typing either.

**The engine filters on dimension names as literal columns.** Dimensions must be in their
derived forms, because the collected forms have no column in the analysis dataset. A chain
can reach stage 5 without this and fail only here.

*Check this on whatever tool you use: it is true of the application described here, at the
pinned commit, and is not a property of the concept model.*
